The hatch lid lifted an inch, and Ines Marroquín noticed it the way she noticed a crack running in sea ice: before her mind had a word for it, her body had already stopped moving.

Tobias was on his knees beside it with the heat gun, swearing at the frozen hinge. He had his left hand flat on the lid. The lid lifted again, against his palm, gently, as if something underneath were testing the weight of him.

"Tobi," she said. "Hand off the hatch."

He looked up at her, annoyed, and the lid went up all at once.

What came through was mostly dark water and cold, and in the middle of it one thing she would remember for the rest of her life: a ridge of pale, overlapping plates, like fingernails grown in rows, opening and closing with a wet click. It closed on Tobias's wrist. There was a sound like a frozen branch breaking under a boot, and then a second, softer sound, a tearing, and Tobias sat back hard on the floor with his arm held up in front of him and no hand on the end of it. The stump was ragged to the bone. White tendon hung from it in two strings. Blood came out of it in a hard, pulsing jet that hit the stove and hissed.

He did not scream. He looked at it with a kind of offended surprise, his mouth open.

Ines was already moving. The plates came up over the lip of the hatch, searching, clicking, and one edge of them caught her face as she lunged past. It did not hurt at first. It felt like being slapped with a wet glove. Then cold air came in where it should not have been, and she understood that her cheek had been laid open from the corner of her mouth to the hinge of her jaw, that she could feel the draught on her back teeth, that the warm sheet running down her neck into her collar was her own blood.

She grabbed the ratchet strap off the sledge hook. She did not think about it. She threw herself on Tobias, got the strap around his forearm above the ruined wrist, and cranked it until he finally did scream, high and thin, and the jet of blood slowed to a heavy drip.

Behind her the hatch was full of water, and the water was rising, and something under it was knocking on the floorboards from below, patiently, one board at a time, working toward the stove.

The radio was on the far wall. The flare gun was in the drawer under it. Between her and both of them, the floor was beginning to lift.

Ines spat a mouthful of blood, felt the flap of her cheek move with it, and dragged Tobias toward the wall by the strap.

The board under her right knee cracked.
